analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal estate tax, gift tax, and generation-skipping transfer tax.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal the estate and gift taxes was introduced in July 1993 with 29 cosponsors and never received a committee vote or floor vote before the Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would eliminate the federal taxes on inheritances, large gifts, and transfers that skip a generation. These taxes apply only to estates above a large value threshold, so the money saved would go almost entirely to heirs of the wealthiest families, while the federal government would lose roughly one percent of its total revenue, as the bill's own findings state. The bill never moved past its initial referral to the tax-writing committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to the largest estates. The estate tax is owed only on estates above a high value threshold, so repeal would direct its savings to the wealthiest families; the bill's own findings note these taxes produced about 1 percent of federal revenue in fiscal 1992 [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the entire federal estate tax, gift tax, and generation-skipping transfer tax, effective for deaths and gifts after enactment [S2][S3].
Its findings argue the taxes force some small businesses and farms to sell assets to pay the bill, and cite estimates that repeal would raise GDP and create jobs [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally. The bill's own text acknowledges these taxes supply about 1 percent of total federal revenue, so repealing them would either deepen the deficit or shift that burden to other taxes paid by people of ordinary means [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill's own findings concede these taxes produce about 1 percent of total federal revenue, so repeal would remove that money from the treasury and force borrowing or offsetting tax increases on everyone else [S3].

The savings would flow overwhelmingly to the largest estates, since these transfer taxes only apply above high value thresholds; smaller estates pay little or nothing, so ordinary families would see no direct benefit from repeal.

The strongest good-faith case for the bill — that heirs of small businesses and farms sometimes sell assets to pay estate taxes — could in principle be addressed with narrower exemptions rather than full repeal of all three transfer taxes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concentrated: it goes to heirs of the wealthiest households, who face these taxes directly. The cost is diffuse: about 1 percent of federal revenue, per the bill's own text, would have to be made up through borrowing or other taxes [S3]. The bill offered no middle ground, such as higher exemptions for family farms and small businesses, opting instead for full repeal of all transfer taxes.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and sat there with no hearing, vote, or floor action until the Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Representative Christopher Cox introduced the bill on July 23, 1993, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day [S1][S5].
Twenty-nine members cosponsored the bill, 26 Republicans and 3 Democrats [S4].
The action history shows no further steps after the referral: no committee vote, no report, and no House floor action before the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, the estate and gift taxes remained in place, preserving roughly 1 percent of federal revenue that all taxpayers would otherwise have had to replace; heirs to the largest estates did not get the repeal they sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal taxpayers generally; wealthy estates lost the repeal

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was overwhelmingly Republican — 26 of 29 cosponsors — with only 3 Democrats signing on, and the Democratic-led Ways and Means Committee never acted on the bill [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Heirs to the largest estates (wealthiest households)
industries.note: These households bear the estate and gift taxes directly, so repeal would have been a direct windfall to them. Their gain would have been paid for by lost federal revenue that everyone else would have to cover through borrowing or other taxes [S3].

industries.industry: Estate planning attorneys and trust services
industries.note: The bill's own findings describe families spending heavily on lawyers and trust structures to avoid these taxes [S3]; full repeal would have eliminated much of that business, while keeping the tax preserves it. This industry's interest neither clearly helps nor clearly costs ordinary people.
